items.title: Leave your coding agent for 5 minutes and most of its cache is gone
items.summary: I measured the public GitHub Copilot coding-agent trace by idle time. At 4 to 5 minutes, 64% of the next prompt is cached. At 5 to 6 minutes, 26%. A long tool run costs the cache as much as a coffee break.

items.title: Winners win because they decide they’ve already won and let reality catch up.
items.content_html:
Share

Some people hate winning.

They picture winners as big egos: self-promoters who’ll win at all costs, then celebrate with their alpha-male bros. Those poor people misunderstand winning.

The reason you want to be a winner isn’t to turn every goal in life into some football game. No. It’s because losing all the time is the worst.

Losers get thrown around like my 3 year old daughter’s rag dolls. They eat scraps. They beg for opportunities. They face constant financial issues. They feel like no one wants them.

I can articulate losing perfectly because I was a born loser.

Never won medals. Never got good grades. Lost money constantly. Gambled to look cool. Believed in luck, hope, and the charitable nature of people.

And it got me f*cking nowhere.

At rock bottom, I found myself begging a bank to take me on as a minimum-wage call center worker. Losing meant I had no confidence. 11 months in, I got laid off. That made me more of a loser because I now expected to lose and get laid off again.

Vicious cycle, man.

One idea eventually took over my brain, and writer Jay Yang articulated it perfectly:

Winners win because they decide they’ve already won and let reality catch up.

Only the delusional have a chance of thriving

It’s not normal to think you’ll win before you have any evidence.

But unless you think this way you’ll become normal by default. That may not sound bad, but remember: the average person is broke, sick, overweight, addicted to Netflix, and stuck in a job they hate. They’re not winning at life.

That sounds harsh and it’s not meant to be.

You must look at the public data on how most people live. You must accept what normality really is. Only then can you be motivated to reject it.

That rejection becomes the foundation of your delusional optimism. And that’s what gets you on the path to winning.

When winning is inevitable, you’ll do everything it takes

It’s 1931. America is broke.

The stock market has crashed. Banks are failing. People have stopped traveling. And when people stop traveling, hotels die.

Conrad Hilton owns hotels. He’s drowning in debt. He’s so broke he borrows money from a bellhop just to eat. One day, he’s flipping through a magazine. He sees a photo of the new Waldorf-Astoria in New York, the biggest, tallest hotel in the world.

A man who can’t pay for lunch has no business dreaming about that hotel.

Hilton cuts out the photo anyway. Across the top, he writes: “The Greatest of Them All.” He slides it under the glass on his desk. Now, every morning, it’s the first thing he sees. Every time he sits down to work, it stares back at him.

He doesn’t hope he’ll own it one day. He decides it’s already his.

The only question left is when. So he does what it takes. He fights his way out of the Depression, one hotel at a time. He rebuilds. He grows. Whenever he walks past the Waldorf, he tips his hat to it, like he’s greeting something that belongs to him.

Years pass. Then a decade. Then more. He starts buying the Waldorf’s bonds. His own board thinks he’s crazy. He keeps buying.

On October 12, 1949, Conrad Hilton takes control of the Waldorf-Astoria. 18 years after he borrowed money from a bellhop to eat. The photo didn’t buy him the hotel. It did something more important.

It made quitting impossible.

When you’ve already decided you’ve won, the hard years aren’t a risk. They’re just the time it takes for reality to catch up.

The trouble is most people don’t go all in.

Instead, they focus on the risks and downsides. They assume it won’t work out. So their brain, using neuroplasticity, wires them to think and act in a way that guarantees they lose before they’ve even started.

When your brain believes the outcome is inevitable, you act differently. Most big goals are hard to achieve. So unless you do everything it takes, nothing will happen.

But you won’t do that unless you sell yourself on why first. Otherwise, as soon as you experience a setback or roadblock, you’ll easily give up because that’s what you expected to happen.

When I share this, people mistake it for affirmations or vision boards.

They mistakenly believe that if they dream big enough, it’ll become reality. That’s not true, though. A dream means nothing unless you’re willing to do everything and give up what you already have.

And you won’t be motivated to act that unreasonably unless you first believe winning is inevitable the way Hilton did.

Winning is in the mind

Modern society thinks the solution to every problem is more information.

But that’s rarely the case. In a world of AI, we’re all drowning in information. Winning has nothing to do with access to information. We all have the same ChatGPT and Claude AI tools already.

Winning happens in the human mind. Most people should forget about consuming more information and focus on how the brain works and training their brain to think differently. It’s hard to understand your brain because reality is distorted.

You can’t stand outside of yourself and look in.

You can’t easily see how you think (by design). So you must force yourself to develop radical awareness. It’s why writing stuff down is so powerful. It shows you how you really think, not how you think you think.

If your mind doesn’t believe at the deepest levels that you will win, you won’t win.

Act like you’ve already won

Acting like you’ve already won gives you quiet confidence.

You’ll show up differently. Your shoulders will be back. You’ll stand up tall. There will be a confidence in your voice.

In sales it’s called matching and mirroring. It’s where you use your physiology and your mind to mirror the behaviors of another person — in this case, a winner. The process of acting makes you become the character even if you’re not winning yet.

The thing about winners is they don’t give up easily.

They go beyond what is reasonable to morph into unreasonable sons of b*tches. They push every action past the point where reasonable people stop, and that’s where unreasonable results come from.

Below the surface of winning is actually an obsession with doing hard things.

The joy of playing hard games and winning is addictive. And the rewards from playing hard games are everything you ever wanted in life and more.

When you act like you’re going to win, you may still lose. But acting like a winner teaches you lessons that help you win faster next time.

When someone refuses to give up, gatekeepers just get out of the way

No one wants to get in the way of a madman.

And that’s what winning looks like. Some people call these people underdogs. I call them psychos. Their weirdness and unpredictability scare people so much that everyone just gets out of the way.

Gatekeepers assume from your wild actions that you must know what you’re doing.

I was like this in banking. I spoke as if every opportunity would happen. I spoke out of turn. I pushed back on people earning 10x my salary. No one did that. They were too afraid. The only reason I did was because I had nothing to lose.

I was already at rock bottom. And if my madman plan backfired, I could always get a job at another bank.

Plus it was fun as f*ck. When people think you’re crazy they kiss your ass. They do things they shouldn’t do. That kind of power, persuasion, and brainwashing is addictive in every sense.

Apple co-founder Steve Jobs did this too. Apple employees called it “The reality distortion field.” It’s the decide-you’ve-already-won mindset applied to a whole team.

Bud Tribble coined the reality distortion term in 1981 during the Macintosh project, inspired by Star Trek.

Through sheer conviction, charisma, and a refusal to accept “no,” Steve would bend people’s sense of what could be done, often pushing teams to hit deadlines or build things they’d insisted were impossible.

It cut both ways: it produced breakthroughs, but it also meant he sometimes ignored hard facts, like when he tried to treat his cancer with diet and juices instead of surgery.

That’s the danger of deciding you’ve already won: you can stop listening to reality altogether. Which is why there’s a secret most people miss.

There’s a secret to winning

This part will blow your mind.

You must be insanely humble to win like this. You must prepare like you’ve never won, and execute like there’s no way you can lose.

The best strategies are paradoxes full of contradictions. So is this one.

Thinking you know all the answers will blow up your life. Everyone ignores you. Thinking you need to be an expert or preparing for the next 5 years also ruins your life. The dance, the winning formula, lies in the middle.

Once you’ve decided you’ve already won and will do whatever it takes, your reality eventually catches up. That creates a winning streak that is more addictive than heroin or watching dancing monkey videos on TikTok with other primates.

You can just f*cking wake up today and decide you’ve already won. You can decide you will win no matter what, and you’ll f*ck around and figure it out.

Winning isn’t about winning for the sake of it. Or being #1 on some useless leaderboard. It’s about getting what you want. It’s about getting the rewards you deserve. It’s about reaching your potential instead of settling for mediocrity.

Start acting like you’ve already won. Like winning is inevitable. Eventually, it will be.

P.S.

I’ve never done this on Substack before.

Likely will never do it again.

But I’ve just “graduated” one of my clients to his first 6-figure month.

So to celebrate...

I have opened ONE spot to come work with me and my inner circle in Fearless Money Makers.

The criteria will be extremely high. I’m looking for a serious person trying to get to 6 or 7 figures in the next 6 months.

Click here now to get the full details

items.title: Custom Voices With Qwen3-TTS
items.content_html:
With my kids I’m currently building a little dungeron crawler and we’re trying to learn a bit about game development along the way. However given that we live in the modern times of increasing capabilities we wanted to get a narrator and voice over.

But we also wanted it to not sound like everyone’s standard AI voices so I looked into what options there are on the table. After some investigation I narrowed down to using Qwen3-TTS which uses voice embeddings for custom voices.

With a bit of creativity you can also do more with those custom voices than appears initially. In case this is of interest to you, this post just covers what we learned and with some examples. You can probably point your agent to it and it can do something with it.

What Qwen Offers

Qwen3 is not the only TTS model in town, and it wans’t even my first choice. We initially used Kokoro. However Qwen3 supports voice cloning and we wanted to have it feel a bit more unique.

In practice it’s a bit tricker though. Qwen3 ships three kinds of models:

  • 1.7B-Base (and 0.6B): clones a voice from a few seconds of reference audio
  • 1.7B-CustomVoice: comes with nine built-in speakers and instructions
  • 1.7B-VoiceDesign: invents a voice from a text description

The base model clones either in context or from the speaker embedding alone but there is no documented way to clone a voice and direct it with instructions. That means unlike the custom voice and voice design models you cannot say “speak sad” or “whisper” with a cloned base model.

At present the official options for a custom voice are fine-tuning Base on a single speaker or to make a clip with VoiceDesign and clone it with Base. That is not all that bad, but it means instructions are gone.

Playing With It

For this blog post I took 28 seconds of me from my talk at PyAI Conf, cut between two pauses so that it starts and ends on a full sentence, and transcribed it with Whisper. The transcript is really only needed for baking but to compare against an already existing voice it’s useful to have it say the same thing as the original recording.

Note that a conference talk recording is not ideal but it works anyways. Which is also a good reminder that you really don’t need a particularly clean recording (or a very long one) to get a halfway convincing version of a person. Particularly when then presented to you on a low quality phone call, it won’t be very hard to trick your grandmother.

The first thing you can do is to blend that recording with another voice. For instance you can use VoiceDesign to make up a voice from a description. For this blog post the designed voice was created like this, with Qwen’s own Python package qwen-tts (pip install qwen-tts, I used 0.1.1), which the rest of the code in this post uses too:

import torch
from qwen_tts import Qwen3TTSModel

kw = dict(device_map="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16, attn_implementation="sdpa")
design = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-VoiceDesign", **kw)
wavs, sr = design.generate_voice_design(
    text=open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), language="English",
    instruct="A man in his forties with a warm, natural, medium-low voice, speaking "
             "clearly and calmly at an easy conversational pace, like someone reading "
             "aloud to a friend.",
)

You can see how the two different voices behave, particularly when blended together:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Voice Embeddings

What Base takes from a recording when cloning from the embedding alone is a speaker embedding which is basically 2048 numbers out of a speaker encoder that was trained. The same voice gets similar numbers and different voices get different ones. Which btw, is also a convenient way to do speaker detection from recordings if you want to! It’s not perfect, but it’s quite helpful for a single audio track recording to tell two speakers apart if you do some basic slicing and dicing (more on that below).

Because it is just a vector, you can do arithmetic on it. For instance a weighted average of two embeddings is a spaker that is somewhere between two voices:

base = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-Base", **kw)

def fingerprint(path):
    prompt = base.create_voice_clone_prompt(ref_audio=path, x_vector_only_mode=True)
    return prompt[0].ref_spk_embedding

def blend(a, b, t):
    a, b = a.float(), b.float()
    mixed = (1 - t) * a + t * b
    return (mixed / mixed.norm() * ((1 - t) * a.norm() + t * b.norm())).to(torch.bfloat16)

armin, designed = fingerprint("voices/armin.flac"), fingerprint("voices/designed.flac")

Here is the same sentence in eleven blends:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Note that it stops sounding like me quite quickly, but it retains some of my features. And it for sure ends up with creating a unique voice regardless. I found some better successes when ensuing that the two voices have similar spectograms (eg: similar “recording setups”). In this recording you can hear that one voice picked up by the lapel mic was a bit hollow compared to the designed voice.

If you like a a voice that comes out, you can bake it back into a new recording that you can then use as reference:

import soundfile as sf

mixed = blend(armin, designed, 0.5)
audio, rate = say(open("voices/transcript.txt").read(), mixed)  # say() is shown further down
sf.write("voices/final.flac", audio, rate)
final = fingerprint("voices/final.flac")

The baked voice does not come back exactly as the blend but it makes handling it easier if you want to. It’s just one voice reference file.

So on the question of using those embeddings for speaker recognition: how good does that work? I took an episode of State of Agentic Coding, the podcast Ben and I record, cut it into 2-second windows one second apart and compared each with an embedding of me form the conference.

Somewhat surprising, but maybe not too surprising using my conference recording clip as the reference this does not work at all with Qwen3. If instead I take the 20 seconds where I introduce myself at the start of the episode as the reference, it gets 98% of the rest right.

On the other hand using a model that was trained for speaker verification instead does manage to pick me up from the conference recording clip. For instance ECAPA, finds me from the conference clip in 97% of the windows.

Here are 20 minutes of that podcast, classified by speaker with the different approaches:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructed Cloned Voices

But the embeddings a very useful for the voice cloning! But how to give them instructions? Base and CustomVoice manipulate the speaker the same way: one vector inserted into the talker’s input sequence. In CustomVoice that vector is a row of the embedding table. In Base it is the x-vector from the speaker encoder, which only Base has. The generation code takes either (voice_clone_prompt is a regular argument of generate), and the transformer weights of the two models are nearly identical. So take the embedding with Base, then hand it to CustomVoice instead of one of its speakers:

cv = Qwen3TTSModel.from_pretrained("Qwen/Qwen3-TTS-12Hz-1.7B-CustomVoice", **kw)

def say(text, xvec, instruct=None, language="English"):
    ids = cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_assistant_text(text)])
    told = [cv._tokenize_texts([cv._build_instruct_text(instruct)])[0]
            if instruct else None]
    voice = {"ref_code": [None], "ref_spk_embedding": [xvec],
             "x_vector_only_mode": [True], "icl_mode": [False]}
    codes, _ = cv.model.generate(
        input_ids=ids, instruct_ids=told, voice_clone_prompt=voice,
        languages=[language], non_streaming_mode=True,
        **cv._merge_generate_kwargs(temperature=0.7, subtalker_temperature=0.7),
    )
    wavs, rate = cv.model.speech_tokenizer.decode([{"audio_codes": codes[0]}])
    return wavs[0], rate

wav, rate = say("I really thought this would work.", armin,
                "Speak in a sad, sorrowful tone, voice low and heavy, on the verge of tears.")

Pick a speaker for the slot, a model and an instruction:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Instructions work on cloned voices, but less reliably than on the built-in speakers, and it depends on the emotion, but honestly, it came out better than I anticipated. Definitely good enough to have some true custom voices for a voice over that don’t necessarily sound like something, someone else has in their game.

Other Fun Math

If a voice is a point in a 2048-dimensional space and blending works we can maybe do some other funny math on it. The obvious one is to try to see if some math can be used to manipulate gender.

To find it I had VoiceDesign create 14 different voices for men and women each. When you then take the average woman minus the average man you can then move any voice along that direction:

women = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/f{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
men = torch.stack([fingerprint(f"design/m{i}.wav") for i in range(14)]).float()
middle = (women.mean(0) + men.mean(0)) / 2
axis = women.mean(0) - men.mean(0)
axis = axis / axis.norm()

def move(xvec, t):
    """Put the voice at position t along the gender axis, keep the rest."""
    x = xvec.float()
    return (x + (t - (x - middle) @ axis) * axis).to(torch.bfloat16)

Here is the result for my clone:

Interactive demo: see the post on the website.

Anyways, that’s that. If you want to play around with Qwen3 TTS I hope this was of some help, and maybe you got some ideas of what to do with the voice embeddings. Use it for good, not evil.

items.title: 40 pieces of advice from 40 years of life
items.content_html:
Share

1. Do extremely hard things.

This one pisses a lot of people off.

They read it as hustle culture or burnout. Chronic underachievers hate doing hard things. They see stress as a problem. They get frustrated easily. They can’t stick at one goal for 5 years. They chase passive income. They day trade in every area of life.

I’m going to be extremely blunt here. Doing hard things is an IQ test. People who want it to be easy, relaxing or slow never reach their potential. In a world of AI, all the easy things are now done by software, automation, and bots.

“Easy” is dead.

And as soon as you get obsessed with one hard thing, take it beyond the point of comfort, and force it to work… your life will work.

It’s a pattern I can’t ignore. Every person I respect does hard things. They outsource all the easy sh*t to a mountain of monkeys. Hard is the cheat code. Sorry.

2. Have a lot of s*x.

Nothing wrong with bonking your brains out. Gotta balance out all the hard things you do with some fun.

3. Study neuroplasticity.

I credit becoming a millionaire to neuroplasticity.

Your brain either works for you or against you. What you repeat daily becomes the foundation for what your brain believes. Intentions don’t mean anything. Your brain only understands past actions. Your identity is formed by action.

So take the actions of your ideal mentor and your brain will rewire itself around that goal. But train your brain to be lazy and procrastinate, and it will help you to compound that identity all the way to loserville and extreme poverty.

4. Master game theory.

Every game in life is rigged.

Building a business, climbing the corporate ladder, real estate, investing in stocks, having a family, learning new skills, etc.

To win these games most people try to work harder. But you only have so many hours in the day and everyone else is already playing the work harder game. You must understand how a life game works to manipulate it in your favor.

That happens when you understand game theory. Biggest lesson I learned studying game theory: Effort spent inside a rigged game gets absorbed by the game.

It also means once you understand a game you can rig it in your favor. The opposite is also true. If you don’t understand the game you’re playing and the incentives, it’ll be rigged against you and you’ll work harder and harder and not win.

5. Focus on making more money, not saving.

You cannot save your way to wealth.

Once you understand inflation and currency debasement, you realize the math is working against you every day. This is why the cost of living feels like it’s rising higher than your income. But once you understand the math it makes sense.

Your skills and experience must be used to make more money. That’s the mindset that builds wealth. And the internet creates leverage to allow you to reach more people faster so you can make more money faster.

Internet leverage works in your favor if you let it.

But most people hide.

They’ve been taught to be invisible out of fear or weird privacy reasons. So the opportunities can’t find them because no one knows they exist. Most people think the solution is to keep asking for permission and applying for opportunities. It isn’t.

The challenge with that approach is every opportunity is now global. You’re competing against everyone else in the world with the same skills and experience. Some of them are probably more talented than you.

Permission-seeking is a losing game by default.

Income = Skills + Experience + Visibility

6. Make decisions because 99% are reversible.

I learned an uncomfortable truth when I hit 40:

Most people don’t actually make decisions. They don’t say yes or no. They say “maybe” or “someday, mate.” And this f*cks up their life. Because the only way to know if an opportunity works is to have a go.

If you really want to be a psycho, the only way to make an opportunity work is to force it to work and not let any other outcome occur.

You avoid decisions because you see risks and downsides.

What you forget is that most risks are manageable. Say yes, try it, and if it doesn’t work, change course. Most decisions can be reversed. So saying yes is better than saying maybe, which only leads to procrastination.

Mental Model = Yes + Pivots

7. Chase your obsession.

To win in life requires intensity.

If you treat every opportunity like a hobby, hedge all your bets and never truly go all in – nothing much happens. You just get ignored because nobody feels anything.

Intensity creates emotion. It forces people to feel your vision/mission. It’s what helps you stand out with no extra skill or talent.

Intensity comes from obsession. It’s going all in. It’s acting like a psycho. It’s embracing your weirdness. It’s being unreasonable enough to believe you can change the world in some small way.

Before you die, it’s worth chasing at least one obsession beyond its reasonable conclusion to see what happens. You’ll be surprised when you do.

8. Hang around high performers.

I shouldn’t admit this, but I spent most of my life hanging around losers – drug addicts, gamblers, alcoholics, sleaze bags, players, etc.

My life changed when I went to a Tony Robbins seminar and he told me to raise my standards. So I did. I raised the bar. I forced myself to hang around optimists and people building stuff. Then I joined paid masterminds.

It changed everything.

You can’t escape mediocrity if you’re not around a handful of people doing the same.

9. Take risks or you’ll get painful regrets.

Society programs you to avoid taking risks.

It’s how they chop you back down to size, force you to follow orders, brainwash you with politics full of hidden agendas and bribes, and get you to settle for second best.

This model works for some people, but if you’re reading this, it likely doesn’t work for you. It didn’t work for me either.

This tweet I once read changed my mind about risk:

Playing it safe isn’t actually safe. You’re just trading the chance of winning for the guarantee of nothing.

Playing it safe looks smart.

But it’s a hidden avoidance of growth and change, which only makes life worse the longer it persists.

If you avoid risks for long enough, you end up with deep regrets about what you could have done with your life. Ouch. Worse than an ana1 probe.

10. Embrace your weirdness.

11. Never try to fit in.

Fitting in is how we all act by default, whether we admit it or not.

Trying to fit in means not saying the wrong thing, adopting other people’s beliefs and opinions, staying small, wearing an approved uniform, talking like a robot, and finishing emails with “kind regards” or “let’s circle back and focus on synergy.”

Fitting in is people-pleasing in disguise.

I learned the hard way in corporate that you can never please everybody. Someone is always pissed off with your decision or opinion. Sometimes they just hate you because of your gender or race, too, which sucks.

The better approach is to refuse to fit in. It’s to be yourself. The personal branding knobs call it authenticity. I just call it being congruent and not lying to people about who you really are. You choose.

12. Believe anything is possible.

Most people don’t believe this truth.

Not because they’re stupid, but because the news and politics trained them to think small and join a tribe. You’re taught to outsource your resourcefulness to a leader, government, or corporation and in return they’ll look after you. Haha.

This is one of the greatest lies ever told.

No person or organisation is looking out for you. They’re focused on looking out for themselves. Once you see this truth you can’t unsee it.

I learned this truth the hard way when I had a client who was a lobbyist in Washington. It became clear that incentives and money drove decisions, not logic or neediness. Save yourself before you can save others.

13. Quit climbing the corporate ladder young.

I didn’t quit climbing the ladder to nowhere until 34.

Too late if you ask me. But better late than never. What changed my mind is I met with senior leaders who’d got to the top. The ones making $1m+ a year salaries and bonuses.

All of them lived in quiet desperation.

They had some money, although they were taxed to oblivion, but they had no free time. The more I spoke to them the more I realized they just wanted a day of zero meetings, but it didn’t exist.

The younger you realize the corporate ladder is a scam, the happier you end up being (can’t wait to tell my two daughters).

14. Pay to get help for big problems.

Going it alone with trial and error is the dumbest strategy in the world.

And I did it for 5 years. Cost me millions of dollars. Eventually, I paid to get help and ended up moving 3 times faster. Speed is critical. Every day you don’t figure out your life’s problems, you waste your precious time which can never be recovered.

Money is a mythical object. It doesn’t come with you when you’re dead.

And you can always make more money through the internet. Since I’ve learned this lesson I’ve spent more than $500,000 on coaching and consulting.

Investing money in yourself is a cheat code. It compounds faster than buying an Airbnb, investing in the S&P 500, or getting another degree or certification that everybody else has already.

Being a tightarse is an extremely expensive mistake.

15. Fix your mindset to fix your finances.

Your income is directly proportional to your level of personal growth. Most people are unwilling to change, so their finances stay the same.

16. Believe the world is working in your favor.

Every failure or rejection is protecting you from something.

A few years back, a colleague stopped me in the hallway to talk about total B.S. It annoyed me. I went to lunch 15 mins late.

During that time a madman drove his car up the footpath outside the office and killed a bunch of people, including a baby.

Had I been on time for lunch I would have been standing on the footpath with my headphones on right where the car would have hit me.

That annoying colleague saved my life. The inconvenience worked in my favor.

17. Study human psychology instead of math.

Human thinking runs the world. Understand your mind and how others think, and you’ll have a cheat code for getting what you want. Feels like Jedi mind control.

18. Ignore opinions from unsuccessful people.

They can find problems with every solution.

19. Nobody is thinking about you.

They’re too busy thinking about themselves. They have too many problems of their own to give two sh*ts about what you posted on InstaBAM.

20. Use money to create good.

Money is a resource for good. Yes, it can be used for evil or to buy luxury junk. But money can be used to do good too. Money isn’t evil in itself. How you use it determines its goodness… and you get to choose.

21. Do work that doesn’t feel like work.

You don’t really wanna sit on a beach and do nothing. Deep down you just want to stop doing boring work, and use your creativity and imagination. Solve for that and you’ll fall in love with working hard. Boring work is the only cancer.

22. Dare to build a personal brand.

Sharing your ideas and experiences attracts people to your world. People carry opportunities – not phones, platforms, or computers.

23. Start a weekly newsletter.

Publish your deepest thinking here. Let it wow a small crowd. Nail the headlines if you want readers.

24. Write online daily.

Use writing as a form of deep thinking. It benefits you even if nobody reads it. Choose only one platform. Master the psychology and culture of that platform. Read a lot of content on that platform. Then write your own posts.

25. It's never the right time to do anything.

It’s either today or it’s a p0rn fantasy. Stop kidding yourself.

26. Build a digital business.

You probably won’t get wealthy and have freedom by earning a salary. A salary lets someone else profit from your work and your unrealised potential.

27. Get good at dealing with uncertainty.

28. Make decisions instead of saying maybe.

A decision is yes or no. Every other outcome is procrastination.

29. Get wealthy then help others.

You can’t help anyone if you’re broke and obsessing over money 24/7.

30. Never become a victim.

Victims are insufferable. Appealing to people’s charitable nature has an extremely low chance of success and is manipulation. Turn a tragedy into a hero’s journey that lets you climb out of rock bottom and inspire people.

31. Never outsource blame.

You own every outcome. Always placing blame on yourself gives you more control, even if somebody else did f*ck up.

32. Never trust a politician.

They’re professional liars. Nice words with no actions. They will try to buy your vote with free central bank money they created from nowhere.

33. Never believe governments fix problems.

They create more problems than they fix.

34. Never believe someone is coming to save you.

The incentives to save you or be your free mentor are extremely low.

35. Plan in decades, execute in days.

The vision should be big. The execution should be extreme.

36. Don’t worry about publishing a book.

Authors are mostly broke. Have you noticed?

The authors who do well have massive pre-built audiences. And monetizing your skills and experience with a $20 book where you don’t get the reader’s contact details has the worst ROI in history.

37. Create proof-of-work.

“Trust me, bro” doesn’t f*cking work anymore. Produce these instead…

Experiments. Results. Testimonials. Case studies.

38. Don’t drink alcohol.

I reached 7 years sober the other day. Never felt better. No losing a day to a hangover. Acting like myself. In control. A good role model for my two daughters. Seeing reality as it is, not through beer goggles.

Alcohol is a perfect lie.

Straight life is the best life.

39. Ego is the enemy.

Realize you don’t know 1/100th of f*ck all. That’s how you win. Think you’re King D*ck and people will run away. Humble people learn. Big egos think they’re too good to learn, so they miss new opportunities and their skills fade.

40. Be cringe.

Cringe = Bravery

Cringe = Doing what already works

I recently crossed 600,000 followers on LinkedIn. And to celebrate, I’m giving you a present. Take a peek at the video I just released.

This might be my best boring hack for anyone growing a business today.
