items.title: Not being unhinged is quietly costing you everything
items.content_html:
Share

This isn’t a how-to post.

It’s a call to arms. It’s a mentor you trust trying to help you have a breakthrough. It’s inspiring if you get it, and tragic if you don’t.

Not being unhinged is quietly costing you everything. Let’s change that.

By unhinged, I don’t mean unstable. I mean saying the true thing everyone else is too polished to say.

Why being unhinged is a cheat code

In 2009, Domino’s Pizza was screwed.

People couldn’t stop posting viral posts about how terrible the pizza was. They became a meme. Things got so bad that when they did taste tests, people gave lower scores to a competitor’s pizza if it came in a Domino’s box. Yuck.

The insufferable corporate playbook would have been to go, “Sir, we’ve now got a new and improved pizza. All-new formula. Try it today for $19.95. You’ll love it.”

But Domino’s is unhinged as f*ck.

They brought on a new marketing chief, Russell Weiner. He’s unhinged. He suggested publicly admitting their pizza needed changing. The CEO was shocked. Then he got it.

They shot ads of focus groups saying their pizza was bad. One customer in an ad called it the worst excuse for pizza they’d ever eaten. Son of a gun.

They went even more unhinged.

Domino’s put billboards in Times-F*cking-Square saying “Our pizza crust is like cardboard.” Surprisingly it worked. Sales went up within days of the ad launch.

From 2009 to 2019 Domino’s stock rose 3,400%.

They even passed Pizza Hut in sales and became the world’s biggest pizza chain. The CEO says to this day, internally, they still play a game of who can find another company that was ever this unhinged. There isn’t one.

Everyone says “My pizza is so damn tasty it’ll blow your mind.” Domino’s said “Our pizza tastes like sh*t and we know it.” And they won because they told the truth.

The truth gets shared. It goes viral. And it’s weird, so more people noticed it.

Being polite would have cost them the company.

The guy who walked away from billions, then told the truth about it

Sahil Lavingia is unhinged.

The guy became the second employee at Pinterest. Luck was on his side. He did everything right. But he thought he could build a better company and started Gumroad. The dumb part was he left before his Pinterest stock vested.

This robbed him of billions of dollars.

But Sahil was optimistic. He stuck his middle finger up at the critics. He thought he was so damn smart. So did his startup team. They thought they’d become a billion-dollar company with 100s of employees.

Sahil was terribly wrong. Nobody felt sorry for him.

At his lowest point, he laid off 70% of his company. The worst part was many of these people were his best friends. They felt betrayed. The TechCrunch publication got a hold of the story and it went public. They smoked Sahil. Rightfully so. Idiot.

His investors told him to shut down his startup Gumroad. They said he should start again and raise money from zero for a new company. At the same time, his former Pinterest colleagues became real billionaires.

The rule in Silicon Valley is you never admit failure. You pivot or sell.

Sahil did the opposite.

He published an essay titled “Reflecting on My Failure to Build a Billion-Dollar Company.” In it, he did the unthinkable. He admitted his failures, said he felt like a failure, explained the truth of the layoffs, and boldly shared how much shame he had about it all.

The essay went mega viral. Some of the biggest names in tech praised it. Overnight he grew a massive audience on social media because of his unhinged essay.

In 2021, he ran a crowdfunding campaign for Gumroad. It raised $5M in 12 hours at a $100M valuation. This is unheard of. The stuff of dreams. Being unhinged got him into some powerful rooms and led him to become an early investor in Notion & Figma.

People polish their story, experience, skills, and resume so much, they end up polishing them all into a turd. Polished is forgettable. Unhinged is never forgotten.

Silence would have cost Sahil the comeback.

Being a people-pleaser ruins your life

I didn’t start out being unhinged.

I was petrified in 2014 as I started writing on LinkedIn. I was worried what my colleagues and boss would think. When the marketing team at my employer called me into their office, I was trembling. I thought I was getting fired.

Oddly, they wanted to praise me, study me, and give me a side gig.

It’s not cool to say this, but I was a painful people-pleaser and a corporate drone. I just said whatever was in fashion, even if I thought it was terrible.

I was a brown-noser to the executive team in the worst way possible. And boy was my nose brown from all the poop.

I kissed ass, smiled, and even ate their sh*t.

I did this because I was afraid. I lived in fear. The job was all I had. The title made me sound half successful at dinner parties. This didn’t last forever though.

Later in my career, my boss fired me unfairly.

I gave everything and got stabbed in the back. All out of jealousy. All because of a dirty trick from a guy whose team catchphrase was “mortgage motivation” – you followed his dumb advice, or he cancelled your ability to pay your mortgage. No joke.

Things started to shift. I started to see the truth. I spent the next 6 months unemployed. Nobody would hire me. A well-known tech recruiter said “A career gap means you’re sh*t.” At least this crazy cat lady was honest.

Then I finally landed a new gig. But it was even worse. Nobody spoke the truth. Everyone was just a puppet. It made me extremely frustrated. Internal colleagues blocked me from clients, and excluded me from meetings. I didn’t hit my sales target.

I had nothing to lose.

So I started calling these mofos out in public and to their faces. I called them smiling assassins. They didn’t know what to do. Nobody had the nerve to do that before. Then my core client refused to work with me because they said we were “too Indian.”

The rage started to build.

Then my new neighbor (a not-for-profit) started to play loud music until late at night, and I couldn’t sleep. I told them to tone it down. Their response?

“We’ve got friends on the council. We can do whatever we want.”

I became more unhinged. I took them through the legal system. I rallied 100s of neighbors to fight their bad behavior. To improve the odds of a win, I took the story to all the major news networks. To my surprise, they all ran the story.

I ended up on a prime-time news segment on the largest breakfast show in Australia with the most well-known TV host in the country.

We lost the legal battle. But we ended up winning and getting peace. The bad neighbor never made a loud noise again.

The more unhinged I became, the more my luck increased.

I didn’t understand at the time what was happening. Nobody taught me the hidden power of being unhinged. I now know being a people-pleaser gets you ignored. Playing it safe is actually the riskiest move of all. It guarantees you nothing.

People notice and respect those who dare to become unhinged. And opportunities flow to you behind closed doors when you do because it’s uncommon.

The reason you’re not unhinged

It’s obvious.

You’re worried what people think of you. When you go to speak you wear your safety pants. You don’t say what you think. You imagine you’ll get cancelled, even though you’re not famous.

So you tell people what they want to hear. You don’t respectfully call out contradictions, lies, or craziness.

You think more about not rocking the boat and paying your mortgage than you do about reaching your potential or creating change.

But what did it buy you?

F*cking nothing. You’re now just a few mortgage payments away from homelessness just like the rest of society. And you’ve got to ask for permission and beg for opportunities. You’ve got to patiently wait your turn until you’re chosen.

Except people dumber and less experienced than you keep getting chosen.

The dumbass on Instagram with tats on his cheeks and missing teeth is making more money and seeing his hillbilly foster kids more than you are. Because he’s unhinged. You’re not. That’s the difference.

And nothing will change until you start being just a little more unhinged. Not maniac-level unhinged, but a tiny bit unhinged.

You’ll make more money being unhinged

Your annual income is a reflection of the opportunities you have access to.

When you don’t have any new opportunities coming your way, you settle for the mediocre one you already have. It’s how people go 40+ years working for the same company when they hate their job.

There were no new offers so they stayed there. They even developed Stockholm syndrome. This is when victims begin to actually admire and like the person who tortured them. They even become loyal to them.

Seems crazy on the surface. But it makes sense when you understand just how much humans crave comfort and certainty.

New opportunities are critical. And you want them to be inbound. To get opportunities you need to be visible to the right people. Not famous, viral, or an influencer. Just moderately seen.

When you’re the same as everyone else you become invisible. When you’re weird it’s uncommon, so you get noticed, even if you’re not that talented.

Inbound opportunities increase your value in the market.

The more the better because now you have choices. Now there’s demand. And now you’re a scarce resource like gold. People have to fight for your yes.

You can say no more easily. And you don’t need to bet the farm on one opportunity and need it to work out perfectly. More opportunities also make you appear higher status. And humans are status creatures so no wonder more people are attracted to you.

When you choose the right opportunities, they put more money in your wallet.

In my case, when I became unhinged, people offered me board positions, investment opportunities, sponsorships, free products and services, ad money, consulting gigs, and paid speaking opportunities as high as $50,000.

Being an invisible, people-pleasing, follow-the-sheep, overly polite human lowers your value in the market. It’s the default and it’s simple to solve.

You can be too unhinged

Wait, what?

In the spirit of being more unhinged, it’s important you get the full truth and not just some unicorn, p*rn fantasy from a dude on the internet. There’s such a thing as being overly unhinged. And when you do, you’ll become like this guy:

Posts full of conspiracy theories. Talking down to people who don’t share the same religion. Making odd comments about women and saying “Maybe it’s the milk or the vaccines.” Not a good idea to do this.

I have another friend who went down the same dark path. He found religion, which is fine. What wasn’t fine was what came next.

He went from having millions of followers to sh*tposting all day and talking politics 24/7. If you don’t share his religion, you’re not just an idiot. You’re going to die a horrible death, you purple-haired Hollywood freak (his voice).

That’s the danger and it’s a bloody big temptation. I suggest you resist the urge the same way you resist injecting heroin each day. Many won’t though. But you must.

Because spreading conspiracy theories and showing zero compassion for your fellow humans is the fastest way to destroy the benefits of being unhinged.

They actively undermine and sabotage your life. That’s why self-awareness and humility are important.

If you think your sh*t doesn’t stink, bad news… it does. Just like mine. Be classy unhinged, not degenerate unhinged.

The compass I use is to not share conspiracy theories, and measure the level of controversy I share. If either of them get too high, I know I’ve become a degenerate.

The rules of being more unhinged

5 years of being unhinged online and in real life taught me these rules:

Say what you think

No filters. No pandering. No worrying about fake cancel culture. No fears of being fired because you posted a picture of a rubber ducky on Instagram that the head of HR didn’t like. Just be yourself.

How you are in SMS messages and on a 1-1 call should be the same as in public.

Leave the swear words in

It’s the trademark of being unhinged. It communicates subtly.

The F-word used to be taboo. Then Mark Manson wrote “The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck.” It became a global bestseller.. The game has changed. Swear words are now everyday language.

Write like you talk.

Drop all the “kind regards” and “circle back” nonsense. What you write should sound the same way you talk.

Stop being afraid to say no

My inbox this morning:

  • “Can you speak at a Dubai conference?”

  • “Can we sponsor your newsletter?”

  • “Can I put a guest post on your Substack?”

  • “Can I pay for you to have coffee with me?”

No. F*ck off. I’m raising a baby. It’s her and nothing else. The default answer is no to everything that isn’t the main thing. No explanation given. No apologies. Zero f*cks given. Just the truth. No. Saying no is unhinged.

Pretend nobody is paying attention

Because they’re not. You’re a nobody just like me. Congrats.

You’ll never be unhinged if you worship opinions. You’re not a witch. You can’t brainwash people to change their minds. You can be freaking Mother Teresa and solve climate change while curing cancer, and a group of people will still hate everything you say and do and call you evil.

Get over it. Get over yourself. You’ll be dead one day. We all will.

Focus on the upside, not the downside

Being unhinged is being slightly optimistic.

Assume it’ll all work out. Assume people will be inspired by your truth rather than outraged. Assume everything is working in your favor.

The unhinged truth sets you free. The downside is smaller than you think. The upside is bigger than you can imagine.

Closing Thought

Being unhinged will make you luckier in life.

And you’ll get more opportunities that lead to more money when you do. You’ll join the top 0.01% when you start speaking the unhinged truth instead of parroting what you think everyone wants to hear.

We can’t resist an unhinged badass. They’re just too s*xy to ignore. Why not you too?

items.title: The quiet life is the most ignored way to succeed
items.content_html:
Share

I’m a millionaire, but most people in my life don’t know.

They call me boring. I don’t go on fancy holidays. I don’t own a loud car with a “f*ck you I’m rich” badge on it. My house is extremely basic (see my Instagram).

And I’m proud of my quiet life.

Today my 3 year old daughter went to daycare. She left the house before I had a chance to see her. This has never happened since she was born. I was heartbroken. I immediately drove to her daycare and parked right out the front of her classroom.

As I approached the building, I could hear her shouting “Daddy, daddy, daddy.” She was confused though.

“Why are you here? Aren’t you supposed to be working?”

I explained to her that she’s the most important thing. Work can wait. I stayed and played with her and her friends. We made a castle with two chairs and a blanket.

All the other parents were at work. Shining their shoes to impress clients. Missing key moments from their children’s lives while they chase a loud job title and strangers’ approval who couldn’t give a damn about them.

My daughter’s best friend is Olivia. Her dad works in a big tech company. If he died on Monday from a heart attack, his employer would have someone else in his seat by the end of the week. None of his colleagues would likely attend his funeral.

That’s what the loud, flashy life buys you.

The quiet life is the most ignored way to succeed, mostly because the people living it rarely talk about it. They find it, fall in love with it, and keep quiet. If I weren’t a writer, I’d probably keep quiet about it too.

The me of 10 years ago would have been horrified by the quiet life I live now. I didn't understand it back then. Now I do, and I want you to understand it too.

Living someone else’s life

I’m obsessed with Hollywood. I love movies and actors.

I’ve realized after several decades that I love actors because most of us are actors in real life. We get great at thinking and acting how everyone else wants us to.

It’s not a conscious decision either. We just kind of fall into it.

On the surface this isn’t a problem. But it becomes a problem later on because when you live someone else’s life, you forget who you are.

That’s what happened to me. I became this banker-actor pretending to care about interest rates and transaction fees when deep down I knew it was all meaningless.

I fell into this life because I wanted my family to be proud of me. Banking sounded like a respectable field. That became my criteria for success.

But I learned to hate my life.

The worst part is I lived in denial. I pretended all the loud dinner parties, big swinging d*cks in big tech, and big bank bonuses mattered.

If you don't consciously choose your path to success in life, by default, you'll accidentally adopt someone else's. It won’t immediately lead to a crisis. Eventually it will though.

And by then it might be too late to change.

Online culture sells you the fake dream of being stinking rich

It’s hard to choose the quiet life when social media tells you to do the opposite.

Everyone is flexing. Everyone is making you feel like you could do and be more. The FOMO is a hangover you wake up to every day. Everyone else is doing better than you, you lazy slob.

But are they doing better?

Some people need status, money, and fame to feel worthy of success. That’s deep insecurity more than it is a roadmap to success.

I once heard someone say this: “Improving is quiet. Impressing is loud.”

The goal isn’t to impress others. It’s to improve yourself quietly every day so that you can impress yourself. When you chase the quiet life, you develop quiet confidence. When you chase the loud life, you end up becoming arrogant.

You’ll feel no need to name and shame

My former boss put a post up about how he thinks R UK OK? Day is important.

It would have been a great post, except he left out the part about how he thinks mental health problems are for p*ssies. See, most people don’t know the truth about him. But I do. He was my boss.

And he treated humans worse than slaves.

In another post he had an indirect crack at me. He said people like me who talk about their toxic bosses and quitting the corporate ladder should have the courage to name and tag their bad boss in the post.

Not doing that meant I was a fake guru and a liar.

The stupid thing is I’m not afraid to tag him at all. My ego would love to warn every human on the planet to get the hell away from this guy. But I don’t do it.

Because when you live the quiet life, you don’t need to name and shame people. You don’t let your ego make decisions for you. I’m fine with quietly knowing he is one of the biggest failures I’ve ever met and his life is absolute misery on the inside.

The quietness of that reality is spectacular.

Secretly, I actually hope he removes the giant pole from his ass and learns the hard way to treat people with love and respect.

Try out the loud rich life to see if you like it

I did.

You don’t have to be rich either. Go to a country club. Have some fancy dinners with rich folks. Go to an entrepreneur event in Silicon Valley. Do a workout at an Equinox gym. Rent a luxury car for a week.

The loud life full of status games seems alluring. I found it empty.

The country club was full of rich boomers making fun of people with dark skin and treating waiters like slaves. The fancy fine dining dinners were trash food full of salt, oil, and sugar. The main course was the same size as my 3 year old’s snack bar.

The entrepreneur event was full of trust fund kids who’d never built anything and wanted strangers to invest in their startups, so they could use the money to go take mushrooms in the jungle for a month.

The fancy gym ended up being full of Instagram influencers taking selfies of their steroid muscles instead of working out. And the luxury cars felt good for about a week and then quickly became no different to a Toyota Camry.

Jim Carrey said it best:

“I think everybody should get rich and famous and do everything they ever dreamed of so they can see that it’s not the answer.”

There’s hidden power in the quiet life

The loud life makes it hard to think.

Your brain is full of other people’s opinions, you buy useless crap to impress people who don’t even like you, and you become a consumer instead of a creator.

Paul Graham taught me (years ago) the power of the quiet life. “Quiet is good for thinking, and thinking is how you get rich.”

In a world of AI, those who can think for themselves will get rich.

I heard a story the other day that illustrates this. A business owner posted a video of a sales call with a lead. Every time he asked the lead a question, the lead typed it into ChatGPT and read out the answer. He had no idea his screen was visible.

That’s your competition. Thinking is now rare. People would rather ask a robot trained on Google SEO 101 content than think about answers to basic questions.

But if thinking can make you rich, you need a lifestyle and environment that can produce that type of thinking. Most people don’t have that.

It’s why I am rebelling.

No more than 10 mins a day of phone screen time. Phone off most of the day. No notifications. 4-hour flow states full of deep work. Lots of writing online (like this) because writing is thinking and it helps you join the dots of ideas.

If wealth is nothing more than solving problems, then the person who can live a quiet life and truly think is going to make the most money.

The quiet life is now a prerequisite for wealth.

Being boring is how you access the good life

The modern human hates to be bored.

It's why they need the slot machine in their pocket to entertain them all day. Then when the dopamine hangover hits, their brains are fried and they’re tired.

Boredom is powerful though.

Everyone knows the way to succeed is to do the boring things well. But when people apply that advice they become bored with life. On the surface, it looks like doing the same thing every day makes you bored.

That’s not it.

Doing the wrong thing every day is what creates bad boredom.

I live a pretty boring life. No one is writing a movie about it. Penguin isn’t getting Ryan Holiday to write a book about it, then selling the rights to Disney so Leonardo DiCaprio can play me in “Catch Tim if you can.”

I thought I’d never get married or have kids. Now I’m married with two kids.

It makes me feel more successful than any car I've owned, revenue number I've hit, or award I've won.

The main difference now is I don’t crave overseas holidays or weekends anymore.

Saturday and Sunday feel the same as Monday. Melbourne, Australia (where I live) feels the same as a beach in Hawaii.

I used to crave time off because I was quietly trying to escape my life. But it never worked because as soon as I came home from travel, I felt dead inside again.

The most depressed I've ever felt was when I went on a holiday to Hollywood.

I met movie stars, walked the red carpet, ate at the Seinfeld hamburger hot spot, etc. The day I had to go back to work felt like a samurai sword stabbing me in the boob.

I didn’t miss Hollywood. No. I just hated my life.

The deeper truth is I chased status symbols because everyone else did. And that’s what led me down the dark path I was on. I had to snap myself out of it.

Living a boring life seems stupid. It seems like you’re wasting your life. But that’s only true if you measure success based on someone else’s version. If you measure success by what you experience, you’ll realize you don’t need all the noise and distractions.

You have to live a quiet life to believe in it.

A quiet life isn’t boring. It’s different. It’s freedom-focused, not status-focused. It’s internal, not external. It’s feeling-based, not ego-based.

When you don’t need much, hitting your goal becomes easier

Half my friends struggle because they’re obsessed with becoming millionaires.

I used to be, too, so I don’t judge them. What I’ve realized is when I strip away all the noise, I don’t need much.

They need a double-story McMansion with a chandelier.

I only need a single-story home in a basic suburb. As a result, my home is almost paid off after 3 years, and they have a $5M loan that could bankrupt them if they lose their primary source of income (hence the added stress).

They need a flashy car, so they get a big car loan and pay it off over 5 years. Then at the end of 5 years they have a balloon payment to make and the desire to get the new model so they can stay relevant.

I drive a simple electric car that costs 1/5th of the price and was paid in cash on day one. I keep the car for at least 10 years because I don’t care how old it looks. So I need fewer cars over my lifetime. And I pay no interest.

They had a $100K wedding. I spent $1000 on my wedding. We spent most of the day in a beautiful park with family, which cost nothing.

Once you strip away all the unnecessary flexing and luxury purchases, you don’t need as much money. So you can get wealthier sooner and, most importantly, retire earlier.

This is part of the reason I was able to retire at 34 from my finance career.

I just hit financial freedom faster by giving up all the status games. Now, looking back, I crave freedom much more than I do looking fake-rich.

When you don’t need to spend as much time making money, it leaves a lot of free time for other things – family, journaling, reading, talking, podcasts, etc.

Those activities all add to the quietness.

And over time that quietness compounds into a level of peace of mind that is indescribable. Someone tell the Lambo bros.

Maybe society has it all wrong

Perhaps wearing a penguin suit every day to an adult daycare while commuting in peak hour traffic to impress people who don’t even care about you to then earn money to buy luxury stuff you don’t need is a bad idea.

It’s also possible I’ve become a 40 year old grandpa. I’ll let you decide.

The quiet life is a different life. Trying to be loud and play status games to get rich is actually a hard game to play. What I love about the quiet life is anyone can achieve it.

The most dangerous people in the world are loud people who are trying to be successful. They will crush you like a bug for a $5 bill.

It’s time to consider a quieter way to succeed.

P.S.

Speaking of “ignored ways to succeed”...

A lot of people create offers these days with Claude and their other robot friends.

Offer looks good.

But nobody buys.

That’s because few do the work necessary to validate the offer before launching.

If you have an offer problem, you can solve it in 19 minutes

items.title: I hate modern cars
items.summary:
I hate modern cars

Modern cars are terrible in many ways: the constant beeping, constant distraction-introducing sounds and visuals, everything on screens, several screens present at once (one behind the wheel, one on the dashboard).

Moreover, they’re packed with features nobody needs. I don’t need electric seat adjustment. There was absolutely nothing wrong with the manual levers. They were faster and they worked even when the battery was dead. Now, every time I want to adjust my seat, I have to spend 50% more time on the action of adjustment, and I also incur the risk of sometimes not being able to do that, depending on the state of the car’s battery. It’s strictly worse in almost all aspects, and I the positive (you can adjust tilt, placement and height using the same electronic lever) is hardly worth it.

The electric seat adjustment is just an instantiation of the wider overengineering and solutionism phenomenon present in modern cars. My car’s battery once died, and I couldn’t push it out of the way, because the electronic handbrake was engaged, and there’s no way to disengage it. The battery is dead, so the parking brake button doesn’t work. (I later found out that there is a way to manually disengage it, but you have to go digging behind a panel – hardly the UX of “simply disengage the big lever”.)

Screens everywhere

This is normal:

This is a mental illness:

Safety

The common argument in favor of new cars is that they’re safer.

In most cases, a car produced in 2020 is safer than a car produced in 1970. However, even that isn’t fully true, because depending on the type of problem you find yourself in, a much heavier and sturdier 70s car might actually be safer for you. For example, in a full frontal collision, the heavier your vehicle, the better your chances of survival. But in terms of safety “features” and general safety design, yes, a 2020s car is a safer vehicle overall.

Is a 2020s car much safer than, say, a 2000s car? I don’t think so. They pack in these safety features that beep at you when the car thinks you’re drifting out of your lane or falling asleep. Sometimes the wheel will fight you to stay in your lane. Fun fact, I once almost had a crash because of this behavior. I was in a curve, and had to straddle two lanes to pass a cyclist, but the wheel tried to yank me back on the lane where the cyclist was, in the middle of a curve at that. I distinctly remember being super pissed about that. Here’s a machine that thinks itself better equipped than me to drive, almost causes me to hit a cyclist, and then, on a straight stretch of road, when I’m testing if it’ll yank me back to the lane if I start drifting not into the opposing lane, but to the shoulder and off the road, it does nothing and happily would allow me to crash off the road.

Most safety gains have been achieved with airbags, general platform stability, good brakes and ABS, things like that. But all these half-baked, half-assed “safety” features are just safety theater, and they don’t meaningfully increase the safety, at least not to justify the sharp pricing and constant annoyance. There’s like 10% of high tech that is useful, which leads me to…

I want 10% of high tech

I don’t know how to best describe my relationship with technology, but I guess it could be called “high tech Luddism”. I mostly hate modern technology, but I love 10% of it.

I basically want a full self driving Golf II.

If I want you to drive, you drive. But don’t get in my way if I don’t want to. But actually do get in my way a little bit, in some specific cases, for example if I’m going to definitely crash, beep at me. But don’t constantly beep at me! Gah!

And for the love of God and all that is holy, please give me manual, physical controls for everything. Don’t try to make everything “extra” and luxurious. I don’t need that. I just need physical knobs and buttons and levers, for very basic features. I don’t want “advanced”. “Advanced” is bad. I want basic, but like, well-thought-out, sensibly built basic.

items.title: Your entire life changes when you realize you’re either an investor or an expense tracker
items.content_html:
Share

Everyone is getting wealthy but you.

That’s how it feels. Let’s be honest. No B.S. Social media makes you feel poor. It’s easy to believe all it takes is a new opportunity or a magical guru to help you escape.

I spent a solid decade spinning my tyres and walking in circles trying to get wealthy. I’ve tried every opportunity online. I shouldn’t admit this, but I even tried filling out surveys for money. I know, dumb.

Getting truly wealthy is misunderstood because when people figure it out, they rarely share it. It’s not that they hoard the information. It’s that they don’t share the breakthrough because they understand wealth is deeply psychological, and most people want to change, but there’s a low chance they will.

The average person will clutch onto their beliefs, and their black-and-white or red- versus-blue thinking until it starves them of oxygen and they end up homeless.

One idea helped me escape that cycle and turn $100K of savings into millions. It works whatever stage of wealth you're at.

Only one type of person gets wealthy

My dad once told me, “You’re either an investor or an expense tracker.”

This advice stuck with me, and I think about it every day. I don’t know where he stole it from, but it contains deep wisdom in a single sentence.

The average person never gets wealthy because they’re an expense tracker. They look at costs. They focus on budgets. They develop a dislike for spending money.

This forces a person to act out of scarcity. They’re accidentally focused on what they lack. This has dangerous consequences. The longer this thinking persists, the more you focus on the downsides of every decision.

You sit there asking yourself “What’s the success rate?” or “What is everyone else doing? What does my mom think? What does the butcher say about stocks?”

If you follow the rabbit hole long enough, you end up outsourcing all of your personal power and control to external, uncontrollable forces. And that’s where wealth goes to die and poverty enters the room and kisses you on the butthole.

Expense tracking leads to focusing on downsides. But building wealth is about focusing on opportunities that have asymmetric upside and limited downsides.

Asymmetric upside doesn't mean you'll win more often. It means when you lose, you lose a little, and when you win, you win big. That's why investors can be wrong most of the time and still get wealthy.

Tracking expenses feels safe.

And safety is extremely comfortable. Investing to get wealthy is different. It’s based on belief. When you believe in something early on it feels risky and leads to discomfort and feeling like it’s a dangerous risk.

Now you know why people fail to invest. It doesn’t feel good. But if you don’t act like an investor you never get wealthy.

"Playing it safe isn't actually safe. You're trading the chance of winning for the guarantee of nothing." – @chrislakin

In a podcast interview years ago, I accidentally said this:

“I lost $1.2M so I could make $10M.”

And I believed every word. When someone hacked my digital wallet and stole $1.2M, it stopped feeling like a loss after a few days. I believed the lessons and the motivation that followed would make me wealthier.

That’s exactly what happened.

When you believe the universe is conspiring in your favor, it reframes how you see risk. When a risk goes wrong it teaches you more than stagnation ever will. This is the investor mindset at its core. The focus is learning, failure, and iteration – not perfectionism and a streak of zero losses.

The investor believes you have to lose in order to eventually win. The expense tracker only wants to spend money if they will win the first time. And the odds of getting wealthy after one attempt are worse than winning the lottery.

Not every loss comes from a bad bet. Sometimes life just takes money from you. How you interpret that moment is what separates investors from expense trackers.

The hidden tax everyone pays

There’s a tax everyone pays, including me. It’s called the ignorance tax, and expense trackers pay the highest rate of anyone.

It’s the cost of missing information. It’s the cost of not figuring out a solution to a problem. This tax isn’t paid in dollars from your savings.

You pay the ignorance tax in:

  • Income streams that didn’t start years ago

  • An investment that could have started paying dividends 6 months ago

  • A painful job that destroys your mental health that you should have quit years ago

The weird part is the ignorance tax is less about what you don’t know, and more about what you f*cking think you already know and actually don’t. It’s a type of delusion that holds people back from becoming humble investors who build wealth.

People think they have their finances together and that they’re “steadily on the path to their goal” when they’re actually stuck and won’t admit it. The only way to stop paying it is to do two things:

  • Wising up and being humble as f*ck by admitting you don’t have it figured out

  • Begin making different and better decisions than before

It requires a person to swallow their pride and that’s not easy to do. It hurts your ego and forces you to change, which are the two things expense trackers hate.

Thinking you have wealth figured out keeps you poor.

Poverty loves indecision

2.5 years ago, I hired a landscaper to clean up my garden and dig trenches to fix a rainwater problem that was causing my house’s foundations to sink.

Everything started out well. He became my best friend. He told me what I wanted to hear. He offered to do extra work for no more money and to go above & beyond.

On the final day of work, I paid him in the morning instead of at the end of the day. Subtle difference. By lunchtime he had skipped town. The job never got finished.

I hassled him for 4 weeks to finish the job. He said he was in hospital.

I later found out he was lying. I got screwed. The mistake cost me about $20,000. I had to finish the job myself, and I’m about as handy around the house as a fart in a bottle.

There were two ways this story could end. Never trust another person again to do work for me, or act like an investor and realize some decisions turn into losses.

The expense tracker gets burned by one expenditure and then carries it to their grave. They assume everyone from that day onwards is a conman, so they overthink every decision and end up making no decision.

This quietly kills them financially. And they don’t even know they’re doing it.

The investor realizes there are no perfect decisions and the world is unpredictable. They expect losses.

The fastest way to destroy wealth potential is to be trapped by indecision. It’s like quicksand for your bank account. Nothing moves. Good opportunities are missed. And years of progress are wasted by not moving at all.

Mark Manson says, “The cost of inaction is usually much higher than the cost of making a wrong choice.”

You're better off making wrong decisions and adjusting than training your brain to do nothing.

Here’s a powerful reframe:

Every decision just leads to a different set of problems.

The expense tracker thinks they can avoid problems if they just do their due diligence, think some more, and speak to more people.

But the investor knows you don’t avoid problems. No. You use problems as opportunities. Because getting good at solving problems is how you create more value in the world. And value is a fancy word for money.

Every decision has tradeoffs. Perfect decisions don’t exist. Decide then pivot if needed because most financial decisions are reversible.

You can’t cut expenses or save your way to wealth

Yet many people are fooled into thinking they can.

There’s only so much you can save before your quality of life is sh*t and you’re eating beans and rice. Inflation, currency devaluation, and the need for higher taxes to fund government debt mean the cost of living only rises.

The interest you get on savings, and the tiny annual pay rise (if any) from a 9-5 job don’t go up fast enough to compete with the above. Saving and expense tracking create an artificial cap.

The only proven strategy to blow past this cap is to focus on making more money. That’s the essence of how an investor thinks.

"People who say 'it's too expensive' have never done the math on staying poor."

(Nobby Kleinman)

You create wealth by making investments.

That’s right… there’s no such thing as something for nothing. Expense trackers struggle to make investments. When money leaves their bank account, it feels like a bullet wound to the neck.

Because they’re not used to making investments or spending serious money, they default to saying “this is too expensive.” That line means they see an investment as an expense, which is their first mistake.

Buying an investment property for $2M seems like a lot of money. And in isolation it is. But if you think like an investor you also consider ROI, which expense trackers conveniently forget.

Investing math is a double-edged sword.

Investing $2M feels expensive. But what about the math of never investing and staying poor? That math is often ignored. What something costs is meaningless without the context of ROI.

“Build the nest egg” is one of the greatest scams of the 21st century

I’m Aussie. We obsess over building the nest egg.

The idea is you hoard money, save every dollar, and build your nest egg. It sounds smart on the surface until you break it down. First, storing wealth in a currency long term is stupidity because of inflation and money printing.

Second, a nest egg assumes your value is fixed. It assumes if you lose everything you can’t rebuild. But you can. Rock bottom, tragedy, and bankruptcy are powerful forms of motivation. The investor knows true wealth isn’t storing money or hoarding assets. True wealth lies in the skills you develop that create money.

Money can disappear overnight.

Skills, experience, and mindset can’t be stolen from you. They stay with you. And thanks to the power of the human mind, if the worst happens and your nest egg is lit on fire… it doesn’t matter. Read that again.

Traditional wealth-building advice says never lose your money. I’m telling you that’s stupid. There’s a statistically high chance you will lose money at some point, especially if you try to get wealthy. The goal isn’t to keep every dollar. It’s to get good at making new dollars if old dollars vanish.

Skills make money.

I once saw this tweet that made me wet my pants: “The scary part about getting older is accumulating enough comfort that you start protecting what you have instead of building what you want.”

That’s how an expense tracker lives. They’re so busy protecting everything that they stop stepping into the arena. They are once again optimizing for extreme comfort instead of growth.

I made this mistake too.

I did everything I could to protect the $100,000 I'd saved from my job. I didn’t want to touch it. But then I realized I couldn’t retire on $100K. I could either hoard the $100K, or use it intelligently to grow my wealth.

Because of the high cost of living here in Australia, I had no choice but to think like an investor – and I’m so glad I did. That $100K has now generated millions of dollars from the skills and experiences I acquired with it.

Thinking like an investor is a subtle choice.

It forces you to take the unconscious thinking driving your money decisions and make it conscious. Otherwise, you’ll be robbed by financial demons that’ll guarantee you never experience the freedom and pleasure of wealth.

items.title: What is Codemode
items.content_html:
More than a year ago I wrote a few posts here that recommended people not to load custom tools into their context (or MCP servers) but to just use more scripts. Most importantly I wrote that Code Is All You Need and I wrote about that MCP needs code. With Pi 1.0 we now added MCP support via Codemode which in some ways is a long time coming, but then also maybe somewhat surprising to some. So I want to share some updated thoughts on this blog on what this all means.

What Are Tools

When a harness like Pi provides tools for an LLM to call, it does so by supplying some tool definitions which then translate into some token structure on the server side. Whether a model is encouraged to call a tool is the result of the reinforcement learning process. Something I wrote about before if you want to learn more.

One of the reasons we strongly lean towards CLI and bash is because it allows easy composition of calls, and because the model also learns how the file system works when it’s trained. So when it invokes a tool like echo foo > /tmp/test.txt the model also learns that after that tool call, there is now a file called test.txt in /tmp.

However bash has one fundamental limitation which is that it can only compose programs that run. And there are some things, which are not programs, but native tools to the LLM and they sort of have to be.

The most obvious example here is read or view_image. If a multimodal model needs to read an image, it cannot use cat for that because the harness needs to inject the actual image payload into the protocol of the LLM.

Another quite vivid example are sub agents. In order to spawn and orchestrate sub agents, it’s tricky to avoid tools that are provided by the harness. While in theory the agent could provide a CLI tool that talks to the outer harness via environment variables and Unix sockets, it’s a rather crude process. It however has another issue, and that is where the code runs.

Brains vs Hands

To better understand that, it’s important to think a bit more about where all the bits and pieces run. There really usually are two different systems involved. The first is the brain, the harness: it runs on one machine. It’s trusted. The second is often the same machine, but it’s really where the tools are executing: the hands. In Pi we now call this the execution environment, but you can think of it as the target of all the operations.

Crucially what is important for us, is that there is a dividing line between the harness brain and the target environment that runs bash and executes the tools.

And splitting this in half has some really important consequences. For a start it means that they are running on different file systems and they have different levels of trust. If you for instance use a sandboxing solution like Gondolin your bash stuff will be sandboxed just fine, but the harness itself will not be.

Orchestrating The Harness

Which brings us to what Codemode really does: it’s a way for the LLM to express and orchestrate complex operations on the harness side, but not the execution environment side. Codemode runs in the harness, in its own sandbox. In case of Pi it’s running in QuickJS within a WASM runtime with intentional limitations: no network, no file system, no timers, limited RAM. The only way is to call more tools. You could also imagine that Codemode could run Scheme or some other language as well.

If you are not familiar with Codemode, it’s basically just a way to issue tool calls from within some language, in our case JavaScript. That allows you to compose those calls without necessarily going through the LLM’s context. Credit for naming goes to our friends at Cloudflare who coined it.

For instance if you issue a bash call as a regular tool call in the LLM, then we only throw the trailing 2000 lines into the context and if the agent wants more, it needs to look at the overflow file itself. If however the agent issues that invocation via Codemode, then the Codemode side gets larger outputs sent structurally.

Most importantly, because Codemode is JavaScript the agent can express concurrent operations and basic workflows. A common way in which you see agents now use this, is to first probe at 5-10 items from some tool response to see what it looks like, and to then write a Codemode script that processes the next n items.

Codemode also allows you to throw state into the transcript! That means that one Codemode invocation can stash away data, that the next call in the session can load again. And remember: this is on the harness host, not the sandbox.

In case of Pi, Codemode also allows you to issue calls that naturally do not make any sense in Pi’s traditional interface. For instance if you want to generate images with an image model or you want to classify some text with a one shot classifier model, those Pi APIs are exposed via Codemode, but not via regular tools where they would just waste context.

What It Looks Like

So now that we talked a bunch about it, it’s probably worth being a bit more explicit about it. Let’s walk ourselves through some invocations of Codemode of recent Pi sessions of mine. Note that none of this code is human written. It’s from real sessions of Pi, just re-indented for your viewing pleasure. The agent starts using Codemode automatically either because it’s a task where the model already naturally picks up that tool, or because a user asked it to.

Note that Codemode is by default only enabled in Pi when MCP is enabled, but you can turn it on with "defaultTools": ["+codemode"] in the settings. Just ask Pi to enable it for you.

Generating Images

Let’s start simple with image generation. Image generation is a feature that Pi supports in the AI SDK core, but it’s not a tool that the agent can use. In the past the only way to use image models has been to write a bespoke extension or to have the agent run node itself and use the internal image APIs. However because we expose quite a few of the internal model APIs within Codemode, it means that the agent can use it:

const [painter] = await models.getAvailableOfType("image");
const result = await models.generateImages(painter, {
  input: [{ type: "text", text: "A cute little puppy sitting on a grassy " +
    "lawn, soft natural light, photorealistic" }],
});
if (result.stopReason !== "stop") return result.errorMessage;

for (const block of result.output) {
  if (block.type === "image") image(block);
  else text(block.text);
}

Note that the call to image() sends the image back as image content to the LLM. On the harness side it feeds it directly into both the agent, as well as onto disk as a temporary artifact in case the agent wants to be able to pass that image back to bash.

Classifying Things

Similar things apply to classifier models such as Jev. They also do not fit well into the workflows of an agent through the typical tools. But rather than making a bespoke tool available, Codemode just allows the agent to reach into the AI SDK and invoke those directly. Here you can see how Jev is used to mass process GitHub issues for a quick sentiment analysis:

const jev = await models.getModelOfType("classifier", "typesafe", "jev-latest");
const r = await tools.bash({
  command: "gh issue list --state open --limit 100 " +
    "--json number,title,body,comments",
});
const issues = JSON.parse(r.output);

const results = await Promise.all(issues.map(async (issue) => {
  const res = await models.classify(jev, {
    state: {
      title: issue.title,
      body: (issue.body || "").slice(0, 4000),
      comments: issue.comments.slice(-5).map(c => c.body.slice(0, 800)),
    },
    questions: {
      sentiment: {
        type: "choice",
        instructions: "What is the overall sentiment of the author towards pi?",
        criteria: {
          positive: "Appreciative, happy, constructive praise",
          neutral: "Matter-of-fact report or request without emotion",
          negative: "Frustrated, annoyed, upset, or angry",
        },
      },
      frustration: {
        type: "score",
        instructions: "How frustrated is the reporter?",
        criteria: ["not at all", "mildly", "clearly frustrated", "very angry"],
      },
      kind: {
        type: "choice",
        instructions: "What kind of issue is this?",
        criteria: {
          bug: "Bug report or regression",
          feature: "Feature request or enhancement",
          question: "Question or support request",
          other: "Docs, discussion, meta, spam",
        },
      },
    },
  });
  if (res.stopReason !== "stop") {
    return { n: issue.number, title: issue.title, error: res.errorMessage };
  }
  return { n: issue.number, title: issue.title, ...res.answers };
}));

store("sentiment_results", results);
return results
  .filter(r => !r.error)
  .sort((a, b) => b.frustration.score - a.frustration.score)
  .slice(0, 12)
  .map(r => `#${r.n} ${r.frustration.score.toFixed(2)} [${r.kind.choice}] ${r.title}`);

Note how in that above example we also call store() which dumps the result of that execution into the session transcript. A future invocation of Codemode can thus read back that result if it wants to.

The Promise.all here is fine, because Pi limits the total number of concurrent tool executions itself to four and maintains a queue for the rest.

A more adventurous example is to use Jev to drive a game engine for debugging purposes:

Codemode with Jev for Game Debugging

Here it knows about my tankctl command and it built itself quickly a minimal harness around it to drive a game loop to assist a user with debugging a problem. Note how it built a 30 step loop in which each step goes back to both the game engine to get a text dump of what’s going on, and then to Jev to determine what to do next:

const jev = await models.getModelOfType("classifier", "typesafe", "jev-latest");
const tank = async (cmd) =>
  (await tools.bash({ command: `tools/tankctl "${cmd}"` })).output;
await tank("start --map assets/maps/night_arena.map");

const questions = {
  action: {
    type: "choice",
    instructions: "You control the tank '@' in a top-down tank game. " +
      "Choose the best next action.",
    criteria: {
      attack: "an enemy has line of sight to you and you can fire at it",
      approach: "no enemy has line of sight; drive toward the nearest enemy",
      dodge: "an enemy shot is heading at you and will hit soon",
      powerup: "a powerup is close and no enemy threatens you",
    },
  },
};

function commandFor(choice, st) {
  const p = st.player;
  const enemy = st.enemies.filter(e => !e.dead)
    .sort((a, b) => (b.los - a.los) || (a.dist - b.dist))[0];
  if (choice === "attack" && enemy) {
    return `fire_at tank ${enemy.id}; frames 30 until clear,damage,kill`;
  }
  if (choice === "dodge") {
    // move perpendicular to the closest incoming shot
    const s = st.projectiles.filter(s => !s.yours)
      .sort((a, b) => a.eta - b.eta)[0];
    const dir = s && Math.abs(s.vel[0]) > Math.abs(s.vel[1])
      ? (p.pos[1] > s.pos[1] ? "+down" : "+up")
      : (p.pos[0] > (s ? s.pos[0] : 0) ? "+right" : "+left");
    return `input ${dir}; frames 20 until damage; input stop`;
  }
  const powerup = st.powerups.filter(u => u.available)
    .sort((a, b) => a.dist - b.dist)[0];
  if (choice === "powerup" && powerup) {
    return `goto ${powerup.pos[0]} ${powerup.pos[1]} 180`;
  }
  return enemy ? `goto ${enemy.pos[0]} ${enemy.pos[1]} 90` : null;
}

const log = [];
for (let step = 0; step < 30; step++) {
  const st = JSON.parse(await tank("state"));
  if (st.state !== "playing") break;
  const threats = st.projectiles
    .filter(s => !s.yours && s.miss_dist < 1.5 && s.eta < 1.5)
    .map(s => `incoming shot dist ${s.dist} eta ${s.eta}s`)
    .join("\n") || "no incoming shots";
  const r = await models.classify(jev, {
    state: { map: await tank("view 8"), threats, hp: st.player.hp },
    questions,
  });
  if (r.stopReason !== "stop") {
    log.push(`#${step} classifier error: ${r.errorMessage}`);
    break;
  }
  const choice = r.answers.action.choice;
  const cmd = commandFor(choice, st);
  if (!cmd) break;
  log.push(`#${step} hp=${st.player.hp} ${choice} -> ${await tank(cmd)}`);
}
return log.join("\n");

Calling MCP Servers

Lastly, Codemode obviously is great for calling MCP servers. And because we do not actually expose any of the MCP tools to the LLM, the agent first uses provided APIs to issue a tool search within Codemode to discover what it might be able to do with the connected servers. This form of progressive discovery makes the whole MCP business work well enough for a lot of use cases today.

Here for instance you can see the agent reach for the Sentry MCP straight away, even without discovering the tools, presumably because it has learned during the RL process already about what the Sentry MCP looks like. But it learns from what we inject into the system prompt, that the Sentry server is available to begin with. It’s not completely guessing here.

const orgs = await tools.mcp__sentry__find_organizations({});
const { organizations } = orgs.structuredContent;
const results = await Promise.allSettled(organizations.map(org =>
  tools.mcp__sentry__find_projects({
    organizationSlug: org.slug,
    regionUrl: org.regionUrl,
  })
));
return organizations.map((org, i) => {
  const r = results[i];
  if (r.status !== "fulfilled") return { org: org.slug, error: String(r.reason) };
  if (r.value.isError) return { org: org.slug, error: r.value.content };
  return {
    org: org.slug,
    projects: r.value.structuredContent.projects.map(p => p.slug),
  };
});

Modern MCP Is A Fight

I really don’t want to talk too much about MCP here, but MCP is in fact a protocol that greatly benefits from Codemode. The problem in parts is that MCP in practice often targets harnesses that do not (yet?) use Codemode. But the tide is shifting. In the meantime, a temporary crutch has been to do what Cloudflare did, and do Codemode within the MCP server. But now we have Codemode in Codemode which is pretty bad. It means double JSON escaping, easy for smaller models to get confused by and the inner code cannot call the outer tools. So if you for instance use the Cloudflare MCP servers in Pi, the agent needs to write JavaScript and funnel it through more JavaScript. This is really not optimal, but it’s also understandable that this is happening:

const accRes = await tools.mcp__cloudflare__execute({
  code: `async () => {
    const r = await cloudflare.request({ method: "GET", path: "/accounts" });
    return r.result.map(a => ({ id: a.id, name: a.name }));
  }`,
});
const accounts = JSON.parse(accRes.content.map(c => c.text).join(""));

const out = [];
for (const account of accounts) {
  const r = await tools.mcp__cloudflare__execute({
    account_id: account.id,
    code: `async () => {
      const r = await cloudflare.request({
        method: "GET",
        path: \`/accounts/\${accountId}/workers/scripts\`,
      });
      return r.result.map(s => ({ id: s.id, modified: s.modified_on }));
    }`,
  });
  out.push({ account: account.name, workers: r.content.map(c => c.text).join("") });
}
return out;

MCP Desires

So to end things off: how well does Codemode work with MCP today? Well … not amazingly well. That’s because MCP servers are not really targeting harnesses that use Codemode yet (though at this point I think most harnesses support it).

For this to work well some recommendations:

  • Structured content: Codemode wants calls to return some nicely formatted JSON. So that needs to come back from the server, and many don’t do that yet. The outputSchema system in MCP is great for that.
  • Consistent results: an interesting failure case is when an MCP server does not return consistent data. For instance because it tries to token optimize things depending on how many items are in the result set. This can cause an initial probe with 5 items to succeed, but then fail when the server returns the maximum batch size.
  • Large binary data: today MCP does not yet support large binary data so quite a few use cases that are really interesting do not work well at all yet. You end up with all kinds of weird workarounds such as pre-signed URLs to allow file uploads then to happen through non MCP channels.
  • Composable tool search: the MCP server might know better than the MCP client which tool is appropriate for a task. But there is no good mechanism today that allows a harness to fan out tool searches across multiple MCP servers. It’s all emergent behavior and it does not scale well to multiple active servers.

Future of Codemode

So where does this leave us? Is this a reversal of what I wrote a year ago where I encouraged CLIs? I don’t think so. In fact, the MCP ecosystem from my perspective picked up on exactly what we pointed out a year ago works: code. But Codemode goes beyond MCP in that it can act as a capable mechanism within the harness to express more freedom for the agent.

There are however also some things that we still need to figure out. For one, durability with Codemode is trickier. We might have to adopt some ideas from durable workflow engines here to snapshot invocations. Or maybe, something like Starlark is a better composition language than JavaScript given its deterministic nature.

Images, binary data and just the inability of this pattern to work with smaller models is also something that needs to be fleshed out. So it’s for sure not a perfect solution yet, but it’s quite a useful pattern that I expect us to leverage more.

items.title: How to articulate your story like the top 0.01%
items.content_html:
Share

Most people are forgettable.

And they don’t even realize it. On the surface, this doesn’t seem like a big problem. As you get older, though, it becomes catastrophic.

I experienced it firsthand. I tried to climb the corporate ladder by keeping my past secret. I didn’t tell anyone about the $50M a year eCommerce business I used to run with my brother. Or my extreme battle with mental illness.

I felt embarrassed. I thought people would judge me.

Then I reached a point in my life where I’d finally had enough. I was sick of asking for permission, waiting for promotions, begging for opportunities, working for free to get mentorship, and always being broke and only having $50 left after payday.

One silly little experience changed my mind.

I went to a Toastmasters event – it’s where amateurs practice public speaking. I went because every time I had to give a talk, I nearly pooed my pants (no joke). But the first time I went I didn’t talk. I was too scared. I just watched.

A guy named Bharat gave a short 7-minute speech that blew me away.

I had goosebumps. I felt inspired. I felt like I could do anything.

After the speech I spoke with him. It turned out he had migrated to Australia and didn’t speak English well. He had a strong Indian accent and experienced a lot of racism. He grew up in a poor family too.

But that speech he gave made him stand out. And his cultural differences were instantly forgotten.

I found out he was off to the world championships of public speaking. On the side he had a business coaching high performers to give powerful speeches. Fast-forward to today, and Bharat is a titan of the tech world.

He earns insane amounts of money. Gets invited into rooms most people could only dream of. And spends his day deciding which inbound opportunities he will accept.

Bharat’s secret: basic storytelling.

Once I saw what he did, I couldn’t unsee it. I became obsessed with storytelling and practiced it every day. It’s how I joined the top 0.01% in my field just like Bharat.

It’s the hidden secret of high performers. And it’ll take you to a place in life that you’ve been trying to reach for decades.

Here’s how to articulate your story, so you can do the same.

“A good storyteller with a decent idea will always have more influence than someone with a great idea who hopes the facts will speak for themselves.” – Morgan Housel

Your stories will get ignored if you don’t do this

I’ve personally taught storytelling to 6000+ people. I see one mistake repeatedly.

Most stories are boring. They are cookie-cutter. They feel like “Once upon a time” type stories which put people to sleep. I used to do the same. Then I learned a strategy that fixes the problem.

Every great story has a surprise.

If there’s no surprise it’s just facts, a report, or a journal entry. So… to articulate your story well, you must start with something interesting. If you start with this, it’s easier to tell stories.

Another option is to start with something weird. For example, I used to work in a strip club. That’s weird. That detail alone is a great place to start a story. It instantly and ethically gets attention. Or another example: I ended up dating one of my co-workers and we joined a cult together and fell in love.

Everyone has interesting or weird parts of their life.

The trouble is most people hide them, so they leave them out of their life story. And nobody’s curiosity is piqued so they end up getting ignored.

The hero's journey makes you sound like a douchebag

The insufferable personal branding folks talk about articulating your story too.

They tell you to create a hero’s journey of your life as if you’re Luke Skywalker in the Star Wars movie. This advice seems smart when you first hear it, but it’s dumb if you think about it from the audience’s perspective.

Telling a story about how you were in a dark place and became a hero makes you sound like a giant douchebag. It ends up just stinking of ego from 50,000 miles away. And people tune you out because you sound like another self-promoting knobhead with a $17 course to sell at the end of the TED Talk. No thanks.

Where the hero’s journey framework goes wrong is it focuses too much on you and all your successes. But success highlight reels are boring. They hide the truth. The opposite is even worse: highlighting all your failures like you’re Will Smith in The Pursuit of Happyness, living in a public toilet with your 5 year old kid.

Too much success = bad
Too much failure p*rn = bad

The real goal of articulating your story is to be honest, humble, authentic, and most importantly, to tell the f*cking truth. This is simple but not easy to do.

I find if you focus on being a storyteller and sharing the raw, unfiltered truth, you’re most likely to tell an engaging story that doesn't turn you into a caricature of yourself

What you can learn from the most powerful sentence ever used in a story

Arguably the most famous sentence in storytelling history is one from Hemingway:

“For sale: baby shoes, never worn.”

Those 6 words tell more of a story than the entire database of Amazon fiction books written in the last 100 years. It’s proof that less is more.

When I first read those 6 words, I felt a wave of emotion. I had a newborn baby at the time. I imagined her in those words. I thought to myself, “What if my little girl didn’t make it?” That’s what sharing emotion does.

I’ve had over 1B views on my stories. And this is the hidden technique I’ve used to hit that milestone.

The stories that move people to action contain emotion.

If people don’t feel anything, your story means nothing. The way to extract the emotion out of a story is to start with “How did this event, person, or thing make me feel?” Here’s an example…

In 2001 I was in high school here in Australia. I came to school one day and found out two planes had hit the World Trade Center.

My good friend Abdullah was locked in a classroom with the other Muslim students for the rest of the week. It was feared the non-Muslim students would retaliate and either punch, or even stab Abdullah with a knife.

To the adults, locking him away seemed like the logical choice.

I was 15 at the time. I didn’t understand the madness. All I knew was I wanted to play soccer with my friend Abdullah and now I couldn’t. It made me sad. At the same time, several of my American family friends lost loved ones in the attacks.

It was the first time in my life I felt grief for two things at once: for the people my family friends had lost, and for my friend being treated like a suspect. I truthfully didn't know how to hold both.

4 weeks ago, I bumped into Abdullah at the shopping centre. 25 years had passed, but I instantly felt the same thing I'd felt that day in 2001. It was the first thought that entered my mind.

Then I noticed a pram behind Abdullah's wife. Inside was his newborn baby. Abdullah looked joyous. I thought to myself, “Perhaps it all worked out in the end.”

But it doesn’t end there…

2 weeks ago a client sent me a text. “Sorry Timbo, I gotta bail man.” I asked him why. He said his PTSD had taken over.

He did a tour of duty in Afghanistan and Iraq after the 2001 attacks. What he’s seen still haunts him. He has dark thoughts. The pain he feels will last a lifetime. He can never be free of it, and that’s the ultimate price he paid.

Weirdly, he said he wouldn’t change anything. He’d do it all again. I got goosebumps reading that message. Some people are so damn selfless, it’s hard to comprehend.

What you just read is raw emotion. Perhaps it made you feel something. And that’s what your storytelling should do.

Recounting emotion creates emotion.

Write your stories down first for this little unknown reason

Articulating your story starts with writing.

Why? Because writing is thinking. Writing your story down forces your brain to think deeply about the events and characters. And it’s how you join the dots of your story to your main point or overarching takeaway.

Stories that aren’t written down first are a jumbled mess.

As you write the stories down, the goal is to write like you talk. No filters. Lots of spelling errors. Dialogue. Slang. Say “mate” if you’re Aussie like me. SMS language. Acronyms like BTW and LOL. This is personality. It’s authenticity.

Once you write your story down it needs an edit with 3 goals in mind:

  1. Say less using fewer words

  2. Make the story simpler

  3. Use 5th grader language

The best stories aren’t the smartest. They’re the stories people actually can understand.

Become a maniac by using non-linear timelines

Telling stories makes you a curator.

The goal isn’t to tell the whole story. The goal is to inspire, entertain, persuade, or teach the reader something. You also want to save the reader time, so it doesn’t take your 20-hour memoir book on Amazon (that no one reads) to tell the story. Non-linear timelines are how you do this.

Chronological timelines are boring as f*ck. They’re predictable.

You can salsa dance around the timeline of your story if you want. You can delete entire decades too. Non-linear timelines create unpredictability. And that makes the audience curious. It gives them dopamine too.

Don’t give a f*ck about opinions

Thinking about what people will think of your story is holding you back.

Haters make you think about hate. They don’t make you articulate a story that helps people. What you focus on becomes a reality. I find it’s better to write a story as an email draft in Gmail and picture myself sending it to a close friend.

Not only should you block out what people will think of your story, but you should go the opposite direction and intend to piss a few people off.

Pandering to people or trying to not offend anyone leads to intellectual poverty.

Good stories challenge people. They make people think. They spark comments. They move people. They present new ideas. They bring back old ideas that got cancelled, and allow for new debate.

What people think of your story is none of your business.

Never wait for story inspiration

A blank page is a knife up your butthole that makes you bleed all over the floor.

Document all your stories in advance. Build a library. I have a section in my note-taking app of every story from my life. I add to it daily. The weird part is the last 3 years of my storytelling library is mostly full of stuff about my two daughters. Ohhhhh….. how times have changed.

The best storytellers are observers.

When you make it a habit to note down your stories you tap into this cheat code. Because when a story happens, you’ll forget it in a few days. And even if you don’t forget it, you’ll forget the tiny details.

And the tiny details of a story are what make it stand out. What you were wearing, where you were, the smell of the air, the feelings, the background characters, the weird objects on the table.

The tiny details make a story come to life. They make it real. They smash any hater who dares say 'that didn't happen' right in the face."

Have a feeling before creating feelings

If you haven’t already got the gist of it, emotion is the #1 goal of a good story. Without it, you have lifeless text and a bunch of empty paragraphs no one will care about. You’ll sound as interesting and as human as a Wikipedia entry from 20 years ago.

One way to create feelings is to first have feelings.

Practically, that means reading an essay or watching a YouTube video that makes you feel something before you get ready to write down or tell your story on stage. I did this just now. I re-read an essay about a man who tries to use AI to save his dying wife of cancer and loses the battle.

It gets me every single time. Especially when he mentions his kids with no mother.

Only after a feeling like that would I dare use stories to create feelings for others. This technique is a superpower. Emotion is a contagious virus worse than the 2020 bat flu.

When you feel something it infects everyone else too. Use it and you’ll have people talking about your stories for decades into the future (and even after you’re dead).

Why most storytelling advice is bullsh*t (including mine)

Wait, what? This is what the storytelling gurus in their white fur coats skip over.

Ready?

Everyone wants to be a somebody, but nobody wants to be the butt-naked person in the middle of the desert with no water, no friends, and wondering if they’ll make it out alive to see their newborn baby.

That’s where stories come from though.

You first have to live the story, which is why so few people have stories to tell. They’re not living. They’re just existing. I got good at storytelling not by reading books or watching storytelling videos on YouTube from famous writers. No. I learned storytelling by having real stories to tell.

I took big risks. Did fake job interviews. Worked in a strip club. Tried to be a famous DJ. Changed jobs every 1-2 years. Went through many romantic breakups. Had $1.2M stolen from my wallet. Started many failed startups. Quit my job. Got fired. Told my boss to F off. Got attacked by 1000s of trolls on LinkedIn, and made it into the LinkedIn Lunatics hall of fame (a place where strangers ridicule you to get likes).

The best storytelling comes from living first, then observing what happened. If you don’t actually put anything out into the world, there’s no story to tell the world.

That’s the detail the gurus skip over. Now you know.

What this all means for you

I always thought storytelling was for broke, romantic writers.

Now I realize that mastering storytelling is how you stop selling, and start subconsciously persuading people to do things you want them to do. This superpower can be used for good or evil. Obviously, I recommend you use it for good like I do.

When you master storytelling, you have opportunities come to you instead of having to ask permission for them. This alone is worth the time it takes to master the skill. And in a world of AI, storytelling is how you stand out. It’s no longer a nice-to-have.

It’s a survival skill.

So…

Articulate your story like the top 0.01% by starting with an interesting idea, adding emotion, and wrapping it in your life experience. You become unf*ckwithable and powerful when you do. That’s the cheat code to life you probably didn’t know.

P.S.

If you can articulate your story like the 0.01%, you can earn like the top 0.01%.

In fact, it’s a core part of my Effortless Sales strategy.

Want to know the rest of it?

I’ve opened my Effortless Sales workshop for enrollment.

In 60 minutes, you’ll get all you need to make effortless sales.

If you’ve got an offer you’re struggling to sell, you need to be at this workshop.

Get all the details here while there’s still time.
